name: Syracuse University

profile.address: 623, Skytop Road, Town of Onondaga, Onondaga County, New York, 13210
profile.reading:
The Green Data Center sits at 623 Skytop Road on Syracuse University's South Campus in the Town of Onondaga, New York, and it is one of the more thoroughly documented examples of sustainable data center design built by an American university. Syracuse University developed the facility in partnership with IBM, completing it in 2009 as a purpose built research computing facility rather than a conventional enterprise data center retrofitted for efficiency after the fact.

What made the project notable at the time, and what continues to draw attention from people studying data center design, was its approach to on site power and thermal management. Rather than drawing all of its electricity from the regional grid and rejecting waste heat outdoors the way a conventional facility does, the Green Data Center was built around on site trigeneration. Natural gas microturbines generate electricity close to where it is used, and the heat those turbines would otherwise waste is instead captured and put to work twice over, first for building heating and second, run through absorption chillers, for cooling the data center floor itself. That combined approach, generating power, heat, and cooling from a single fuel source on site, is intended to reduce both reliance on the regional power grid and overall energy waste compared with a conventional design that treats power, heating, and cooling as three separate systems.

The project drew contemporaneous coverage in trade publications including Campus Technology and Cabling Installation and Maintenance as an early, concrete example of a university committing capital to sustainable data center infrastructure rather than treating efficiency as an afterthought, at a time when the broader data center industry was only beginning to treat energy efficiency as a design priority rather than a marketing talking point. Syracuse University's research computing division continues to describe the Green Data Center as central to the university's high performance and research computing capacity, meaning it primarily serves Syracuse's own faculty and student research computing needs rather than operating as a commercial colocation facility for outside tenants.

Syracuse University has not published a specific critical IT load figure in megawatts for the facility, and no independent public record reviewed here supplies exact square footage or construction cost either. For a facility built specifically as a case study in sustainable design, that gap is somewhat notable. What is well established instead is the engineering approach itself. This is an on campus, IBM partnered research computing facility that generates its own power on site and reuses the resulting waste heat for both heating and cooling, built in 2009 as one of the earlier examples of a university applying combined heat and power design directly to a data center rather than only to general campus buildings.
